title: Host staging priority imbalance — case studies and mitigation notes
summary: Working notes from a set of small experiments showing that low-priority host staging threads (PCIe reads to satisfy tensor slices) can create long-tail latency spikes for multi-GPU inference pipelines. Documents observed modes, microbenchmarks, and mitigations we should evaluate in the runtime.
motivation: We periodically see sporadic p99/p999 spikes in production for medium-sized chat requests (~1k tokens) on 8x A100 boxes. Hypothesis: contention between inference work and host-side staging I/O (page faults / PCIe reads) where low-priority worker threads are preempted or throttled, allowing request-handling paths to stall waiting for staged data.
environment: Test cluster: 2x DGX-A100 (8x A100 80GB) nodes connected via 100GbE + NVLink fabric. PCIe between host and GPU is Gen4 x16; NVidia driver 535.x, CUDA 12.3, NCCL 2.16. Runtime build: infer-runtime v0.38.0 (local profiling build). OS: Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 5.15 with preemptible desktop scheduling. Workloads: 1) many small concurrent requests (QPS 120), 2) single large-context request (6k tokens) running pipeline/tensor-sliced model (12-way tensor shards + 2-pipeline stages).
methodology: Repro steps summarized: 1) baseline latency profile with no background IO; 2) introduce synthetic NVMe/PCIe read workload to emulate host-side staging; 3) vary staging-thread niceness/rt priority (nice/chrt) and CPU pinning; 4) toggle use of io_uring vs pread/preadv; 5) measure end-to-end latency distributions (median, p95, p99, p999) and collect perf traces (sched_switch, block_rq_issue, pread latency), nvprof+nsys for GPU-side stalls, and tcpdump/strace for request timing. Microbenchmarks for read size: 4KB, 64KB, 2MB; for batch sizes: 1, 4, 16. Each test ran for 15 minutes and repeated 3x to ensure variance.
experiment_results: Baseline (no extra IO): median 22ms, p95 48ms, p99 120ms. When low-priority host staging threads run (nice +19, default SCHED_OTHER): median 24ms (+9%), p95 62ms, p99 380ms, p999 spikes to 1.2s observed. When staging threads are promoted to SCHED_FIFO with modest rt priority (50): median 25ms, p95 54ms, p99 128ms — almost baseline but with fewer 1s spikes. Using io_uring for staging reduced CPU syscalls and dropped p99 by ~30% relative to pread under same priority. PCIe read amplification (many small reads) increased host CPU overhead and correlated with p99 growth; aggregating reads (2MB contiguous) shortened median and tail substantially. On pipeline-sliced workloads the effect amplified: small interleaved slices caused repeated host pulls and each preemption cascaded across pipeline stages, creating multi-hop stall amplification (one slow stage stalls downstream replicas).

Notes: multiple retries where staging thread was chased off CPU by background processes; observed many pread syscalls returning only partial data requiring multiple round-trips.
root_causes: Host-side staging implemented with many small synchronous reads (4KB-64KB) => high syscall rate and PCIe read amplification
Staging threads run at default niceness and get preempted by other system activity (cron, kubelet, monitoring agents) causing long waits
Pipeline/tensor-sliced workloads magnify single-stage stalls because downstream stages are blocked waiting on upstream I/O
OS scheduler and IRQ affinity are suboptimal: NVMe queues and staging thread CPUs are not pinned, leading to cache misses and migrations
mitigations_explored: Promote staging threads to SCHED_FIFO with bounded RT priority (tested priority 40-60) — large tail reduction but RT threads must be watchdoged
Switch staging path to async io_uring batching with pre-registered buffers to reduce syscall overhead and partial reads
Aggregate small reads into larger DMA-friendly chunks (2MB) when safe — reduced PCIe read amplification
CPU pinning: reserve 1-2 isolated cores for staging and pin NVMe IRQs to same cores
NUMA-aware placement: ensure staging threads and request handlers share NUMA node with PCIe root to lower latency
Increase prefetch window in runtime so fewer host round trips are necessary (trade memory for tail reduction)
Consider GPUDirect/peer-DMA where available to avoid host bounce for certain topologies
tradeoffs_and_risks: RT scheduling reduces tail but makes debugging harder and can starve other system services. Aggregating reads increases memory footprint (prefetch buffers) and risks wasting bandwidth if prefetch heuristics are wrong. io_uring adoption is promising but requires careful buffer lifecycle management to avoid double-copy. CPU isolation reduces consolidation efficiency and can increase cost. GPUDirect requires hardware and driver support and may not be portable across all deployments (private vs hosted).

unresolved_questions: What is the minimum safe prefetch size for transformer shard reads without wasting memory for the largest models we serve?
Can NCCL scheduling be adjusted to hide upstream staging variance (e.g., asynchronous fine-grained signaling)?
Do cloud-hosted Dedicated boxes expose IRQ/NVMe controls necessary for CPU pinning guidance?

notes_to_self: Next run: repeat tests with reduced background monitoring (disable node_exporter) to verify noise floor. Also capture nvlink counters during spikes to see if staging stalls correlate with increased NVLink retransmit. Good candidate for a short slide for infra sync — show before/after graphs.
conclusions: Host-side staging priority and the size/pattern of PCIe reads are first-order contributors to long-tail latency in multi-GPU inference pipelines. Practical short-term mitigations (io_uring, staging thread promotion, CPU pinning, read aggregation) produce meaningful tail reductions. Longer-term work should aim to reduce number of host round trips (prefetch, smarter shard packing) and investigate direct-GPU-data paths where feasible.
